column14: option_a
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which sentence best describes cellular respiration?
column14: The lungs pull air in and push air out
column15: A cell splits in two to make two new cells
column16: Cells break down glucose using oxygen and store the released energy in ATP
column17: Cells use sunlight to build sugar out of carbon dioxide and water
column28: Cellular respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells: glucose and oxygen are broken down into carbon dioxide and water, and the released energy is stored in ATP. Building sugar with sunlight is photosynthesis, moving air is breathing, and splitting in two is cell division. The most common mix-up is thinking cellular respiration means breathing.
column29: Think about what happens to food molecules inside your cells, not in your lungs.

column9: The sugar that your cells break down as their main fuel in cellular respiration is called ___.
column28: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is the sugar cells break down for energy. Starch and table sugar are digested into glucose first. A common mistake is writing ATP; ATP is what the cell makes, not the fuel it starts with.
column29: It's the same sugar plants make in photosynthesis and doctors measure in your blood.

column9: In cellular respiration, glucose reacts with a gas from the air called ___.
column28: Oxygen (O₂) is the gas that reacts with glucose. You breathe it in and your blood carries it to your cells. A common mistake is writing carbon dioxide, which is the gas respiration gives off, not the one it uses.
column29: It's the gas you would run short of if you held your breath.

column9: Compared with the air you breathe in, the air you breathe out contains more of which gas, because your cells make it during cellular respiration?
column14: Oxygen
column16: Helium
column17: Carbon dioxide
column28: Your cells release carbon dioxide as a waste product of cellular respiration. Blood carries it to your lungs and you breathe it out. Exhaled air actually has less oxygen, because your cells used some of it. Nitrogen passes in and out unchanged.
column29: Which gas is made by the reaction, not used up by it?

column9: Select every product of aerobic cellular respiration. Select all that apply.
column14: Glucose
column16: Carbon dioxide
column17: ATP (usable energy)
column28: Products are what the reaction makes: carbon dioxide, water, and ATP. Glucose and oxygen are the reactants that get used up. Sunlight is used in photosynthesis, not respiration. The common mistake is picking oxygen, which is a product of photosynthesis, not of respiration.
column29: Products are written on the right side of the arrow: what gets made, not what gets used.

column9: Your thigh muscle cells use huge amounts of ATP when you climb stairs. Which organelle would you expect to find in especially large numbers in these cells?
column14: Cell walls
column16: Chloroplasts
column17: Mitochondria
column28: Most of the ATP from cellular respiration is made inside mitochondria, so cells that use a lot of energy, like muscle cells, are packed with them. Animal cells have no chloroplasts or cell walls. A common mistake is choosing chloroplasts; they capture light energy in plants and don't run on glucose for your muscles.
column29: Which organelle runs the later stages of cellular respiration?

column9: In a chemical equation, which side of the arrow shows the reactants?
column14: The right side: the substances that get made
column15: The left side: the substances that get used up
column16: Both sides: the substances that never change
column17: Neither side: reactants are written above the arrow
column28: Reactants are the starting materials, so they go on the left of the arrow. Products are made, so they go on the right. In respiration, glucose and oxygen are on the left. Students sometimes flip the two because the arrow points toward the products.
column29: Read an equation like a sentence: starting materials ... turn into ... what's made.

column9: The first stage of cellular respiration, which splits glucose in half in the cytoplasm, is called ___.
column28: Glycolysis means "sugar splitting." It breaks glucose in half in the cytoplasm and makes a small amount of ATP (net 2). The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain come after it, inside the mitochondria. A common mistake is writing Krebs cycle, which is the second stage.
column29: "Glyco" means sugar and "lysis" means splitting.

column9: How does the oxygen your cells use for cellular respiration get to them?
column14: Your stomach makes it from the food you eat
column15: It soaks in through your skin from the water you drink
column16: Your cells make it out of carbon dioxide
column17: You breathe it in, and your blood carries it from your lungs to your cells
column28: Oxygen enters your lungs when you breathe in, moves into your blood, and is carried to every cell. Food supplies glucose, not oxygen. Cells can't turn carbon dioxide back into oxygen; plants do that in photosynthesis.
column29: Which body systems move air and blood?

column9: Where does the glucose your brain cells use for cellular respiration come from?
column14: Your brain cells make glucose from sunlight
column15: Your digestive system breaks carbohydrates in food into glucose, and your blood delivers it
column16: Your lungs pull glucose out of the air
column17: Your cells make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, the way plants do
column28: Glucose comes from the food you eat. Your digestive system breaks carbohydrates down into glucose, which is absorbed into your blood and carried to your cells. Air has no glucose, and only plants and other photosynthesizers build glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
column29: Think about what happens to a sandwich after you eat it.

column9: A mushroom growing on a fallen log has no chloroplasts and cannot do photosynthesis. How does the mushroom get the ATP it needs?
column14: It makes ATP from sunlight that hits its cap
column15: It doesn't need ATP because it doesn't move
column16: It breaks down sugars it absorbs from the rotting log through cellular respiration
column17: It absorbs ready-made ATP from the soil
column28: Fungi like mushrooms absorb food from what they grow on and break it down by cellular respiration to make ATP. Every living cell needs ATP, even if it doesn't move. Without chloroplasts, the mushroom can't use sunlight at all.
column29: Every living thing needs ATP. Where would a mushroom get its fuel?

column9: Cellular respiration is often described as the "reverse" of which process?
column14: Mitosis
column16: Digestion
column17: Diffusion
column28: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide, water, and light to make glucose and oxygen. Respiration uses glucose and oxygen to make carbon dioxide, water, and ATP. The products of one are the reactants of the other. Digestion breaks food down, but it doesn't use oxygen to make ATP.
column29: Which process has the same chemicals as respiration, just on opposite sides of the arrow?

column9: When do the cells in your body carry out cellular respiration?
column14: All the time, even while you sleep, because cells always need ATP
column16: Only while you are exercising
column17: Only when you are breathing fast
column28: Your cells use ATP every second to stay alive (pumping ions, building proteins, keeping your heart beating), so respiration never stops. Exercise and eating change how fast it happens, not whether it happens.
column29: Does your heart stop needing energy when you fall asleep?

column9: Match each substance to its role in cellular respiration.
column14: Glucose :: The fuel molecule that gets broken down
column15: Oxygen :: The gas taken in and used up to release the fuel's energy
column16: Carbon dioxide :: The waste gas carried to your lungs and breathed out
column17: ATP :: The energy carrier that cells spend to do work
column28: Glucose is the fuel and oxygen is used up as it's broken down; those are the reactants. Carbon dioxide is the waste gas you exhale, and ATP holds the captured energy; those are products. A common mix-up is switching oxygen and carbon dioxide.
column29: Two of these go in and two come out. Start with the fuel.

column9: When a cell uses ATP for energy, it breaks off one phosphate group. The molecule left behind, which has two phosphate groups, is called ___.
column28: ADP (adenosine diphosphate) has two phosphates. Cellular respiration uses energy from glucose to add the phosphate back, turning ADP into ATP again. A common mistake is writing AMP, which has only one phosphate.
column29: "Tri" means three. What prefix means two?

column9: Which of these is a reactant of cellular respiration?
column14: Water
column16: Carbon dioxide
column17: Glucose
column28: Glucose is a reactant: it is used up as the fuel. Carbon dioxide, water, and ATP are all products made by the reaction. A common mistake is choosing water because it shows up in photosynthesis as a reactant.
column29: A reactant is something the cell needs to start the reaction.

column9: Which word equation shows aerobic cellular respiration?
column14: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP
column16: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
column17: glucose → oxygen + ATP
column28: Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen and makes carbon dioxide, water, and ATP. carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen is photosynthesis, the reverse of respiration. A common mistake is choosing it because it has the right substances, just on the wrong sides.
column29: Start with the fuel and the gas you breathe in.

column9: A firefly's glowing tail, a cheetah's leg muscles, and the nerve cells in your brain all get their energy DIRECTLY from which molecule?
column14: Glucose
column16: ATP
column17: Oxygen
column28: ATP is the molecule cells spend directly to do work like making light, contracting muscles, and sending nerve signals. Glucose stores energy, but cells must first convert it into ATP through cellular respiration. The common mistake is picking glucose because it's the original source.
column29: Glucose is the fuel tank. What's the cash the cell actually spends?

column9: About how many ATP molecules can aerobic cellular respiration make from ONE molecule of glucose? (Use the number in the respiration equation from class.)
column28: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + 36 ATP. Some textbooks say up to 38, so 36–38 is accepted. A common mistake is answering 2, which is only what glycolysis gives by itself.
column29: It's the number written at the end of the respiration equation in your notes.

column9: ATP stands for adenosine triphosphate. The prefix "tri" tells you that each ATP molecule has three ___ groups.
column28: ATP has three phosphate groups. Breaking the bond to the last one releases energy and leaves ADP (two phosphates). A common mistake is writing "adenosine"; there is only one adenosine in each ATP.
column29: Look at the end of the word triphosphate.

column9: Select every cell job that is powered by ATP. Select all that apply.
column14: Contracting a muscle cell
column16: Oxygen diffusing into the cell
column17: Water moving into the cell by osmosis
column19: Pumping molecules across the membrane by active transport
column28: Active transport, muscle contraction, building proteins, and sending nerve signals all need ATP. Diffusion and osmosis are passive: molecules move from high to low concentration on their own, so no ATP is spent. The common mistake is thinking every movement in a cell costs energy.
column29: Remember from Unit 3: which kinds of transport are passive?

column9: What kind of energy is stored in the bonds of a glucose molecule?
column14: Nuclear energy
column16: Light energy
column17: Chemical energy
column28: Energy stored in the bonds between atoms is chemical energy. Cellular respiration releases it and stores it as chemical energy in ATP. Plants captured it from light energy, which is why light energy is a tempting wrong answer.
column29: It's the same kind of energy stored in gasoline and batteries.

column9: A goldfish in a bowl needs oxygen for cellular respiration. Where does its oxygen come from?
column14: The carbon dioxide the fish gives off
column15: The gravel at the bottom of the bowl
column16: The fish food sprinkled on top of the water
column17: Oxygen gas dissolved in the water, taken in through its gills
column28: Water holds dissolved oxygen gas. A fish's gills pull that oxygen into its blood, just like your lungs do with air. Food gives the fish glucose, not oxygen, and carbon dioxide is a waste product, not a source of oxygen.
column29: Fish don't have lungs. What part of a fish does the same job?

column9: On a cold morning you can see your breath as a small cloud. Part of that cloud is tiny droplets of which product of cellular respiration?
column14: Oxygen
column16: Water
column17: Glucose
column28: Cellular respiration makes water. Some of it leaves your body as water vapor in your breath, which condenses into a visible cloud in cold air. Glucose is a reactant, oxygen is a reactant, and ATP stays inside your cells.
column29: Which product can be a gas, a liquid, or a solid depending on temperature?

column9: Cellular respiration is a chemical reaction. What does that tell you about the atoms in glucose and oxygen?
column14: They are rearranged into new substances, carbon dioxide and water
column15: They are destroyed to make energy
column16: They turn into brand-new atoms that make up ATP
column17: They stay exactly the same and just melt into a liquid
column28: In a chemical reaction, atoms are not created or destroyed; they are rearranged into new substances. The carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms end up in carbon dioxide and water. A common mistake is thinking the atoms turn into energy. The energy comes from the bonds, not from destroying atoms.
column29: Can atoms be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction?

column9: Where does cellular respiration take place?
column14: Only in the blood
column16: Inside the cells of the body
column17: Only in the lungs
column28: Cellular respiration happens inside cells, mostly in their mitochondria. The lungs only exchange gases, the stomach digests food, and the blood delivers supplies. The common mistake is choosing lungs because the word respiration is also used for breathing.
column29: The answer is hiding in the name: CELLULAR respiration.

column9: Select every one of these that carries out cellular respiration. Select all that apply.
column14: A wind-up toy
column16: A maple tree
column17: A robin
column28: Every living thing, including plants, animals, and fungi like mold, carries out cellular respiration to make ATP. Rocks and toys are not alive and have no cells. A common mistake is leaving out the tree because plants also do photosynthesis.
column29: Pick everything that is alive, even the ones that make their own food.

column9: How many carbon atoms are in one molecule of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆?
column28: The subscript 6 after C means 6 carbon atoms. Glucose also has 12 hydrogen atoms and 6 oxygen atoms. A common mistake is adding all the subscripts (24), which counts every atom, not just carbon.
column29: Look at the small number right after the C.

column9: Match each substance in the respiration equation to its chemical formula.
column14: Glucose :: C₆H₁₂O₆
column16: Carbon dioxide :: CO₂
column17: Water :: H₂O
column28: Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆, oxygen gas is O₂, carbon dioxide is CO₂, and water is H₂O. A common mistake is mixing up O₂ and CO₂; carbon dioxide has a carbon (C) in front.
column29: "Di" means two. Which molecule has one carbon and two oxygens?

column9: Cellular respiration produces oxygen.
column28: False. Cellular respiration USES oxygen; it produces carbon dioxide, water, and ATP. Oxygen is produced by photosynthesis. Mixing up the two processes is the most common mistake.
column29: Is oxygen on the left or right side of the respiration equation?

column9: Cells make ATP during cellular respiration and then use it up as they do work.
column28: True. ATP is made during respiration and spent to power cell work. When it's used, it becomes ADP, which respiration recharges back into ATP. A common mistake is thinking ATP is stored for a long time; cells make and use it constantly.
column29: Think of ATP like money you earn and spend every day.

column9: A rechargeable battery is a good model for ATP and ADP. In this model, what "recharges" ADP back into ATP?
column14: Energy released when glucose is broken down in cellular respiration
column16: Sunlight hitting the cell directly
column17: Carbon dioxide entering the cell
column28: ATP is the charged battery and ADP is the used one. Energy released from glucose during cellular respiration adds a phosphate to ADP, recharging it to ATP. Animal cells can't use sunlight directly, and carbon dioxide is a waste product, not an energy source.
column29: Which molecule holds the energy that respiration releases?

column9: Which body system carries food molecules and gases to every cell so the cells can carry out cellular respiration?
column14: Nervous system
column16: Skeletal system
column17: Circulatory system
column28: The circulatory system (heart, blood, and blood vessels) delivers glucose and oxygen to every cell and carries carbon dioxide away. The digestive and respiratory systems supply those molecules, but blood is what delivers them. The nervous system sends signals, not supplies.
column29: What flows through your body and reaches every single cell?

column9: A car engine burns gasoline with oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide and water. If you compare a car engine to a cell doing cellular respiration, the gasoline matches which molecule?
column14: Carbon dioxide
column16: Glucose
column17: Water
column28: Gasoline is the car's fuel, just as glucose is the cell's fuel. Both react with oxygen and give off carbon dioxide and water. The difference is that the cell captures much of the energy in ATP instead of letting it all out as heat. A common mistake is matching gasoline to oxygen because both go into the engine.
column29: Which molecule is the fuel that gets broken down?

column9: A bean seed sprouting underground has no leaves yet. Why does it still need cellular respiration?
column14: To make ATP for growing, by breaking down food stored in the seed
column15: To soak up sunlight through the soil
column16: It doesn't; seeds don't respire until they have leaves
column17: To make oxygen for the soil
column28: A seed stores food. As it sprouts, its cells break that food down by cellular respiration to make the ATP needed to grow roots and a shoot. Respiration uses oxygen; it doesn't make it. A common mistake is thinking plants only get energy once they can photosynthesize.
column29: Growing takes energy. Where does a seed with no leaves get its fuel?

column9: During cellular respiration, energy is passed from one molecule to another. Which arrow shows the correct direction?
column14: Glucose → ATP
column16: ATP → oxygen
column17: Carbon dioxide → glucose
column28: Respiration takes the energy stored in glucose and stores it in ATP, which the cell can spend. Moving energy from carbon dioxide into glucose is photosynthesis. A common mistake is picking ATP → glucose, which is backward.
column29: Which molecule is the fuel, and which is the ready-to-spend energy?

column9: Why do you get hungry and need to keep eating every day?
column14: Food turns directly into ATP in your stomach
column15: Your cells only carry out respiration while you eat
column16: Your cells constantly use up glucose in cellular respiration, so the fuel supply has to be replaced
column17: Your stomach needs food to store oxygen
column28: Your cells are always breaking down glucose to make ATP, so the supply runs low and must be refilled by eating. Food is digested into glucose first; it doesn't become ATP in the stomach. Cells respire all the time, not only during meals.
column29: What do your cells keep burning through, day and night?

column9: Bromothymol blue (BTB) turns from blue to yellow when carbon dioxide is added. A student breathes out through a straw into a tube of blue BTB, and it turns yellow. What does this show?
column14: Exhaled breath contains carbon dioxide made by cellular respiration
column16: The water in the tube evaporated
column17: BTB makes carbon dioxide when it is shaken
column28: The color change shows carbon dioxide was added, and the only source was the student's breath. That carbon dioxide was made by the student's cells during cellular respiration. A common mistake is thinking the yellow color means oxygen.
column29: Reread what BTB reacts to.

column9: Some of the energy released during cellular respiration is not captured in ATP. What happens to it?
column14: It is destroyed
column15: It is given off as heat, which helps keep your body warm
column16: It is turned into oxygen
column17: It is stored back in glucose
column28: No energy change is 100% efficient. The energy not captured in ATP is released as heat, which is why your body stays warm and heats up during exercise. Energy can't be destroyed; it only changes form.
column29: Why do you get hot when you run?

column9: A black bear hibernates all winter without eating. What are its cells breaking down for cellular respiration during that time?
column14: Oxygen alone, with no fuel at all
column15: Stored body fat and other stored food
column16: Nothing; its cells stop respiring
column17: Snow that it eats
column28: A hibernating bear lives off the fat it stored in the fall. Its cells break those stored molecules down to make ATP, but slowly, because its body has slowed down. Oxygen alone can't make ATP; there must be fuel. Its cells never stop respiring, or it would die.
column29: Why do bears eat so much in the fall?

column9: Which activity would make your muscle cells carry out cellular respiration FASTER than they do while you sit and read?
column14: Sitting still
column15: Riding a bike up a steep hill
column16: Sleeping
column17: Watching TV
column28: Working muscles need much more ATP, so they break down glucose faster, which uses more oxygen and makes more carbon dioxide. Sleeping, sitting, and watching TV all use less energy than reading at a desk, or about the same.
column29: Which choice takes the most muscle work?

column9: A cow eats only grass. Where did the energy in the glucose the cow's cells break down originally come from?
column14: Minerals in the soil
column15: Sunlight captured by the grass during photosynthesis
column16: The cow's own mitochondria
column17: The water the cow drinks
column28: The grass captured light energy and stored it in glucose by photosynthesis. The cow eats the grass, digests it, and releases that stored energy through cellular respiration. Mitochondria release energy; they don't create it.
column29: Trace the energy back one step before the grass.

column9: A monarch butterfly sips sugary nectar from flowers. How does the nectar help the butterfly fly?
column14: The nectar is stored in its wings as ATP
column15: Its cells break down the sugar in cellular respiration to make ATP for its flight muscles
column16: Sugar slows down cellular respiration so it saves energy
column17: The sugar gives the butterfly oxygen
column28: Nectar sugar is fuel. The butterfly's cells break it down by cellular respiration and use the energy to make ATP, which powers its flight muscles. Sugar contains no oxygen gas, and food is not stored as ATP.
column29: What is sugar to a cell: fuel, oxygen, or waste?

column9: The cells in a carrot root grow underground and have no chloroplasts. How do they get ATP?
column14: By cellular respiration, using sugar sent down from the leaves
column15: By making ATP from light that leaks through the soil
column16: They don't need ATP because roots don't move
column17: By absorbing ATP from the soil
column28: Leaves make sugar by photosynthesis and send it down to the roots. Root cells break that sugar down by cellular respiration to make ATP for growing and for pulling minerals in from the soil. Every living cell needs ATP, even ones that don't move.
column29: Root cells can't photosynthesize. Where does their fuel come from?

column9: A cross-country runner eats a big plate of pasta the night before a race. How does this help during the race?
column14: Pasta slows down cellular respiration so the runner doesn't tire
column15: The starch is digested into glucose, giving muscle cells more fuel for cellular respiration
column16: Pasta gives the runner extra oxygen
column17: Pasta contains ready-made ATP for the muscles
column28: Starch is a carbohydrate made of glucose units. The runner digests it and stores the glucose, which muscle cells break down during the race to make ATP. Food doesn't contain usable ATP or oxygen gas.
column29: What is starch made of?

column9: A student says, "Cellular respiration is just another name for breathing." Which statement best corrects this?
column14: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; cellular respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that uses that oxygen to release energy from glucose
column15: They are the same thing, and both happen only in the lungs
column16: Cellular respiration happens only in plants, while breathing happens in animals
column17: Breathing makes ATP, while cellular respiration moves air
column28: Breathing is the physical movement of air; cellular respiration is the chemical reaction inside every cell. They're connected: breathing brings in the oxygen respiration needs and removes the carbon dioxide it makes. ATP is made in cells, not lungs.
column29: Where does each one happen: lungs or cells?

column9: Cyanide is a poison that stops mitochondria from using oxygen. Why can even a small dose be deadly?
column14: It stops the lungs from making carbon dioxide
column15: It makes cells produce too much glucose
column16: It makes cells produce extra ATP until they overheat
column17: Cells can no longer finish aerobic respiration, so they quickly run short of ATP
column28: Without using oxygen, the mitochondria can't finish aerobic respiration, so ATP production crashes. Heart and brain cells need so much ATP that they fail within minutes. A common mistake is thinking the problem is the lungs; the lungs still work, but the cells can't use the oxygen.
column29: What does oxygen allow the mitochondria to make?

column9: Which stage of aerobic cellular respiration makes the most ATP?
column14: Glycolysis
column16: Krebs cycle
column17: Electron transport chain
column28: The electron transport chain makes about 32 of the 36 ATP. Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle each make only 2. Digestion isn't a stage of cellular respiration at all; it happens in your gut before glucose reaches your cells.
column29: Think about the last stage, the one that uses oxygen.

column9: How many molecules of oxygen (O₂) are needed to completely break down 4 molecules of glucose by aerobic respiration?
column28: Each glucose needs 6 O₂ (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → ...). So 4 glucose × 6 O₂ = 24 O₂. A common mistake is answering 6 or 10 by forgetting to multiply.
column29: Find how many O₂ one glucose needs, then scale up.

column9: A cell completely breaks down 3 glucose molecules by aerobic respiration. How many molecules of carbon dioxide does it produce?
column28: Each glucose makes 6 CO₂, so 3 × 6 = 18. You can also think of it as carbon atoms: 3 glucose × 6 carbons = 18 carbons, and each CO₂ holds one carbon. A common mistake is answering 6.
column29: Every carbon atom in glucose leaves in its own CO₂ molecule.

column9: Put the steps of aerobic cellular respiration in order, from first to last.
column14: Electron transport chain
column16: Glucose enters the cell
column17: Glycolysis
column28: Glucose enters the cell, glycolysis splits it into pyruvate in the cytoplasm, pyruvate moves into the mitochondria, the Krebs cycle releases CO₂ and loads energy carriers, and the electron transport chain uses oxygen to make most of the ATP. A common mistake is putting the Krebs cycle before glycolysis.
column29: Glucose has to be split before anything can go into the mitochondria.

column9: Sprouting bean seeds are sealed in a jar with gas sensors. Over two days, what changes would you expect in the air in the jar?
column14: Nothing changes, because seeds don't respire
column15: Both oxygen and carbon dioxide go up
column16: Oxygen goes up and carbon dioxide goes down
column17: Oxygen goes down and carbon dioxide goes up
column28: Sprouting seeds carry out cellular respiration, so they use up oxygen and give off carbon dioxide. The reverse would happen only during photosynthesis, and sprouting seeds in a jar have no leaves to do much of it. A common mistake is thinking seeds are not alive until they grow leaves.
column29: Which gas is a reactant, and which is a product?

column9: How are the products of photosynthesis related to cellular respiration?
column14: They are the reactants that cellular respiration uses
column15: They have nothing to do with cellular respiration
column16: They are the same as the products of cellular respiration
column17: They are waste that cellular respiration can't use
column28: Photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen, which are exactly the reactants of cellular respiration. Respiration makes carbon dioxide and water, which are the reactants of photosynthesis. The two processes form a cycle.
column29: Write both equations, one under the other, and compare the sides.

column9: Hummingbirds beat their wings about 50 times per second. Compared with a resting box turtle of the same body mass, a hummingbird's cells would most likely...
column14: use glucose and oxygen much faster and give off more carbon dioxide
column15: use less oxygen, because the bird is so small
column16: stop cellular respiration while flying
column17: make their own glucose from the air
column28: Flying takes huge amounts of ATP, so the hummingbird's cells run cellular respiration very fast: more glucose and oxygen in, more carbon dioxide and water out. That's why hummingbirds must feed constantly. Being small doesn't mean using less; per gram, a hummingbird uses far more energy than a turtle.
column29: More work means more ATP. What does making more ATP use up?

column9: Which statement about energy in cellular respiration is correct?
column14: Cellular respiration uses up energy without releasing any
column16: Cellular respiration turns matter into energy, so atoms disappear
column17: Chemical energy in glucose is converted into chemical energy in ATP, and some is lost as heat
column28: Energy can't be created or destroyed. Respiration moves chemical energy from glucose into ATP, and some leaks out as heat. Atoms are rearranged, not destroyed. The common mistake is saying respiration "makes energy"; it releases energy that was already stored.
column29: Can energy be created? Can atoms disappear?

column9: Which statements about aerobic cellular respiration are true? Select all that apply.
column14: It makes glucose
column16: It uses oxygen
column17: It happens only in animals
column18: In plant and animal cells, most of it takes place in mitochondria
column28: Aerobic respiration happens inside cells, mostly in mitochondria; it uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. It breaks glucose down rather than making it; that's photosynthesis. Plants, fungi, and many microbes do it too, not just animals (bacteria do it without mitochondria).
column29: Check each statement against the equation and against which organisms have mitochondria.

column9: During a long bike ride, your breathing rate and heart rate both go up. How does this help your leg muscle cells?
column14: It brings ready-made ATP from the lungs to the muscles
column15: It cools the muscles so they can stop respiring
column16: It delivers more carbon dioxide to the muscles
column17: It delivers more oxygen and glucose for respiration and removes the extra carbon dioxide faster
column28: Working muscles do more cellular respiration, so they need more reactants (oxygen and glucose) and make more waste (carbon dioxide). Faster breathing and a faster heart deliver supplies and carry waste away. ATP is made inside the muscle cells; it isn't shipped from the lungs.
column29: Think about the reactants going in and the waste coming out.

column9: Fill in the missing product: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6___ + 6H₂O + ATP
column28: The missing product is CO₂, carbon dioxide. Six are made because glucose has six carbon atoms. A common mistake is writing O₂, which is a reactant, already on the left side.
column29: Glucose's carbon atoms have to go somewhere on the product side.

column9: How many hydrogen atoms are in 6H₂O (six molecules of water)?
column28: Each H₂O has 2 hydrogen atoms, so 6 × 2 = 12. That matches the 12 hydrogens in one glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆), which is why the equation balances. A common mistake is answering 8 by adding 6 + 2.
column29: Multiply the coefficient by the subscript.

column9: One glucose molecule gives 36 ATP in aerobic respiration. How many ATP can a cell make from 5 glucose molecules?
column28: 5 glucose × 36 ATP each = 180 ATP. A common mistake is adding (36 + 5 = 41) instead of multiplying.
column29: Each glucose gives the same amount. How many groups of 36?

column9: How many atoms in total (carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen together) are in one glucose molecule, C₆H₁₂O₆?
column28: 6 carbon + 12 hydrogen + 6 oxygen = 24 atoms. A common mistake is answering 3, which is the number of different elements, not the number of atoms.
column29: Add all three subscripts.

column9: Which equation for cellular respiration is correctly balanced?
column14: C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
column16: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
column17: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 3O₂ → 3CO₂ + 3H₂O
column28: With 6O₂, 6CO₂, and 6H₂O, both sides have 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen, and 18 oxygen atoms. The equation with no coefficients is unbalanced, and the one with 3s leaves carbon unbalanced. The 6CO₂ + 6H₂O equation is balanced but it's photosynthesis, not respiration.
column29: Check carbon first: glucose has 6.

column9: Why does the respiration equation need 6O₂, 6CO₂, and 6H₂O instead of just one of each?
column14: To make the equation look neater
column15: Because cells always react molecules in groups of six
column16: Because the cell makes 6 ATP
column17: So the same number of each kind of atom appears on both sides, because atoms aren't created or destroyed
column28: The coefficients balance the equation. Glucose has 6 carbons, so 6 CO₂ are needed to hold them; it has 12 hydrogens, so 6 H₂O are needed; then 6 O₂ supply the rest of the oxygen. This follows the law of conservation of matter.
column29: Count carbon atoms on each side with and without the 6s.

column9: The Krebs cycle is also known as the...
column14: cell cycle
column16: Calvin cycle
column17: water cycle
column28: The Krebs cycle is also called the citric acid cycle, after the first molecule it forms. The Calvin cycle is part of photosynthesis, and the cell cycle is how cells grow and divide. Mixing up Krebs and Calvin is the most common mistake.
column29: One of these names includes a molecule found in lemons and oranges.

column9: In the first stage of cellular respiration, one glucose molecule is split into two molecules of...
column14: water
column16: oxygen
column17: carbon dioxide
column28: Glycolysis splits one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules. Carbon dioxide isn't released until pyruvate enters the mitochondria. A common mistake is choosing carbon dioxide because it is the final carbon product.
column29: It's the molecule that then moves into the mitochondria.

column9: Which statement correctly describes how energy moves through photosynthesis and cellular respiration?
column14: Photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose; cellular respiration releases that energy into ATP
column15: Photosynthesis turns ATP into light energy
column16: Cellular respiration stores light energy in glucose; photosynthesis releases it
column17: Both processes build glucose from light energy
column28: Photosynthesis captures light energy and stores it as chemical energy in glucose. Cellular respiration releases that stored energy and captures it in ATP. Reversing the two is the most common mistake.
column29: Which process needs the sun? Which process makes ATP from food?

column9: A class measures how much carbon dioxide crickets give off at three temperatures: 10 °C: 0.2 mL/min, 20 °C: 0.5 mL/min, 30 °C: 0.9 mL/min. What is the best conclusion?
column14: The crickets' rate of cellular respiration increased as the temperature increased
column15: Temperature had no effect on the crickets
column16: The crickets stopped respiring at 10 °C
column17: The crickets took in carbon dioxide at warmer temperatures
column28: Carbon dioxide is a product of respiration, so more CO₂ per minute means faster respiration. The CO₂ rose with temperature. Crickets are cold-blooded, so warmth speeds up their body chemistry. The crickets still gave off CO₂ at 10 °C, so they didn't stop respiring.
column29: What does carbon dioxide output tell you about respiration?

column9: A student claims, "Plant cells don't need mitochondria because they have chloroplasts." Which evidence best shows the claim is wrong?
column14: Plant cells contain mitochondria, and plants give off carbon dioxide in the dark
column16: Chloroplasts make carbon dioxide
column17: Plants never use ATP
column28: Chloroplasts make glucose, but plant cells still need mitochondria to break that glucose down into ATP. In the dark, when no photosynthesis happens, plants give off carbon dioxide from respiration. Plants use ATP for growth and transport just like animals do.
column29: What would you measure from a plant in the dark?

column9: A heart muscle cell contains thousands of mitochondria, while a skin cell on your arm has far fewer. What does this difference suggest?
column14: Skin cells carry out more cellular respiration than heart cells
column15: Heart muscle cells need much more ATP, because they work nonstop
column16: Mitochondria store water for the heart
column17: Heart cells are older than skin cells
column28: More mitochondria means more cellular respiration and more ATP. The heart beats nonstop for your whole life, so its cells need enormous amounts of ATP. Skin cells do much less work. Mitochondria make ATP; they don't store water.
column29: What do mitochondria produce, and which cell uses more of it?

column9: In the equation C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP, what does the 6 in front of O₂ mean?
column14: Six ATP molecules are made
column15: Six molecules of oxygen gas are used for each glucose molecule
column16: There are six atoms in one oxygen molecule
column17: Oxygen is used six times faster than glucose
column28: A coefficient (the big number in front) tells how many molecules. So 6O₂ means six molecules of oxygen gas react with one glucose. The small subscript 2 tells how many atoms are in each molecule. Confusing coefficients with subscripts is the common mistake.
column29: Big numbers in front count molecules; small numbers after count atoms.

column9: Why don't cells use glucose directly to power their work, instead of making ATP first?
column14: Glucose contains no energy at all
column16: One glucose holds a lot of energy at once, so cells repackage it into many small ATP "packets" they can spend where needed
column17: Cells have no way to take in glucose from the blood
column28: Glucose is like a $100 bill and ATP is like a handful of $1 coins. Cell jobs need small, quick payments, so respiration breaks glucose's large energy store into about 36 ATP. Glucose definitely has energy, it's a normal, safe molecule in your blood, and cells take it in from the blood all the time.
column29: Think about breaking a big bill into small change.

column9: At night, a houseplant can't carry out photosynthesis. What gas exchange is happening in its leaves?
column14: It takes in oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide, from cellular respiration
column16: No gas exchange happens until the sun rises
column17: It takes in carbon dioxide and gives off oxygen
column28: Plants carry out cellular respiration all the time. In the dark, with no photosynthesis covering it up, you can see only respiration: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out. Taking in CO₂ and giving off O₂ is photosynthesis, which needs light.
column29: Which process never stops, day or night?

column9: Students seal a sprouting pea in one tube of blue BTB and a glass bead the same size in a second tube of BTB. Why include the tube with the glass bead?
column14: To make the experiment finish faster
column15: As a control, to show that any color change comes from the living pea, not from the tube or the BTB
column16: To give the pea extra oxygen
column17: Because glass beads also carry out cellular respiration
column28: The glass bead tube is the control: it has everything except a living thing. If only the pea tube turns yellow, the carbon dioxide must have come from the pea's respiration. A glass bead isn't alive and can't respire.
column29: What would you compare the pea tube to?

column9: Desert kangaroo rats can live their whole lives without drinking water. Much of the water they need is made inside their own cells. Which process makes that water?
column14: Digesting sand
column15: Photosynthesis, which happens in their fur
column16: Diffusion of water out of the cells
column17: Cellular respiration, which produces water as glucose is broken down
column28: Water is a product of cellular respiration (6 H₂O per glucose). Kangaroo rats eat dry seeds, and the water their cells make while breaking down that food meets most of their needs. Animals don't do photosynthesis.
column29: Look at the products of the respiration equation.

column9: Which two stages of cellular respiration take place inside the mitochondria?
column14: Glycolysis and the electron transport chain
column15: The Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain
column16: Glycolysis only
column17: Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle
column28: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm. The pyruvate it makes moves into the mitochondria, where the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain finish the job. A common mistake is placing glycolysis in the mitochondria.
column29: The first stage happens before anything enters the mitochondria.

column9: During which stage of aerobic cellular respiration is oxygen (O₂) actually used?
column14: Electron transport chain
column16: Krebs cycle
column17: All three stages use it equally
column28: Oxygen is used only at the end of the electron transport chain, where it accepts electrons. Glycolysis doesn't need oxygen at all. The Krebs cycle depends on the chain to keep running, but it doesn't use O₂ directly. The common mistake is thinking oxygen is used in every stage.
column29: Oxygen waits at the very end of the process.

column9: In which stage are the carbon atoms from glucose mostly released as carbon dioxide?
column14: None; carbon stays in ATP
column16: Glycolysis
column17: Krebs cycle
column28: Carbon leaves as CO₂ after pyruvate enters the mitochondria, mostly during the Krebs cycle. Glycolysis only splits glucose in half without releasing any CO₂, and the electron transport chain makes water, not CO₂. ATP is an energy carrier that gets recharged; glucose's carbon atoms don't end up in it.
column29: Which stage was described as releasing CO₂ in your notes?

column9: What happens to oxygen at the end of the electron transport chain?
column14: It combines with carbon to form carbon dioxide
column16: It accepts electrons and combines with hydrogen to form water
column17: It becomes part of ATP
column28: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. At the end of the chain it picks up electrons and hydrogen ions and becomes water (H₂O). The oxygen in exhaled CO₂ comes from glucose and other molecules, not from the O₂ you breathe. Choosing carbon dioxide is the most common mistake.
column29: Which product of respiration contains hydrogen and oxygen?

column9: NADH and FADH₂ are made during the Krebs cycle. What do they carry to the electron transport chain?
column14: Oxygen gas
column16: Glucose
column17: High-energy electrons
column28: NADH and FADH₂ are energy carriers. They bring high-energy electrons (with hydrogen) to the electron transport chain, which uses that energy to make most of the ATP. Carbon dioxide is released as waste; it isn't carried anywhere.
column29: The electron transport chain needs a supply of what?

column9: When a person loses 10 pounds of body fat, where does most of that mass go?
column14: It turns into muscle
column15: It is converted into pure energy
column16: It leaves only as sweat
column17: It is breathed out as carbon dioxide, with the rest leaving as water
column28: When fat is broken down by cellular respiration, its carbon atoms leave as CO₂ (breathed out) and its hydrogen atoms leave as water. Studies show most of the mass is exhaled. Matter can't turn into energy in a chemical reaction; the energy comes from bonds, not from atoms vanishing. Sweat is mostly water you drank.
column29: Follow the carbon atoms. Which product holds them?

column9: Count the oxygen atoms on the reactant side of C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. How many are there in all?
column28: Glucose has 6 oxygen atoms, and 6O₂ has 6 × 2 = 12. Total: 6 + 12 = 18. The product side also has 18 (12 in 6CO₂ + 6 in 6H₂O), so oxygen balances. A common mistake is answering 12 by forgetting the oxygen inside glucose.
column29: Don't forget glucose has oxygen atoms too.

column9: A cell made 108 ATP by aerobic respiration, at 36 ATP per glucose. How many molecules of O₂ did it use?
column28: First find the glucose: 108 ÷ 36 = 3 glucose. Each glucose uses 6 O₂, so 3 × 6 = 18 O₂. A common mistake is stopping at 3, which is the number of glucose molecules, not oxygen molecules.
column29: Two steps: how many glucose, then how many O₂ per glucose.

column9: A sample of cells gave off 30 molecules of CO₂ by aerobic respiration. How many glucose molecules were completely broken down?
column28: Each glucose makes 6 CO₂, so 30 ÷ 6 = 5 glucose. A common mistake is multiplying (180) instead of dividing.
column29: Work backward from the ratio of glucose to CO₂.

column9: Glycolysis makes a net of 2 ATP and the Krebs cycle makes 2 ATP from one glucose. If the total is 36 ATP, how many ATP come from the electron transport chain?
column28: 36 − 2 − 2 = 32. The electron transport chain makes by far the most ATP, which is why it matters so much that oxygen is there to keep it running. A common mistake is subtracting only one of the 2s and getting 34.
column29: Subtract both of the earlier stages from the total.

column9: Put these steps in order to follow one oxygen atom from the air you breathe to the end of cellular respiration.
column14: Oxygen is used at the end of the electron transport chain and becomes part of water
column16: Blood carries the oxygen to a muscle cell, where it diffuses in
column17: Oxygen diffuses from the lungs into the blood
column18: Oxygen is breathed into the lungs
column28: Oxygen goes lungs → blood → body cell → mitochondrion → electron transport chain, where it becomes part of water. A common mistake is thinking the oxygen ends up in exhaled CO₂; the oxygen you breathe in ends up in water.
column29: Start outside the body and work inward to the last stage.

column9: Put these steps in order to follow one carbon atom from a bite of bread to the air you breathe out.
column14: CO₂ diffuses into the blood and is breathed out of the lungs
column16: Glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into the blood
column17: Glycolysis splits the glucose into pyruvate in the cytoplasm
column18: Starch in the bread is digested into glucose
column19: In the mitochondria, the carbon is released as CO₂
column28: Digestion makes glucose, blood delivers it, glycolysis splits it in the cytoplasm, and the carbon leaves as CO₂ in the mitochondria (mostly in the Krebs cycle). The CO₂ then travels back to the lungs. A common mistake is putting glycolysis inside the mitochondria.
column29: The carbon must be digested, delivered, and split before it can leave as a gas.

column9: A burning marshmallow and a cell doing cellular respiration both turn sugar and oxygen into carbon dioxide and water. What is the key difference?
column14: Burning releases the energy all at once as heat and light; respiration releases it in small steps so much of it can be captured in ATP
column16: Burning makes ATP but respiration doesn't
column17: They make completely different products
column28: Both reactions have the same reactants and products. The difference is control: a fire releases all the energy at once, while cells break glucose down step by step through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain so they can capture it in ATP. Fire captures no ATP at all.
column29: Compare the products first. If they're the same, what's left to differ?

column9: Three sealed tubes of blue BTB sit in a dark cabinet overnight. BTB turns yellow when carbon dioxide is added. Tube 1 has a water snail, Tube 2 has an elodea water plant, and Tube 3 has only BTB. In the morning, Tubes 1 and 2 are yellow and Tube 3 is still blue. What is the best explanation for Tube 2?
column14: The snail's carbon dioxide leaked into Tube 2
column15: The plant made oxygen, and oxygen turns BTB yellow
column16: In the dark the plant could only do cellular respiration, so it released carbon dioxide
column17: The plant absorbed the blue color from the water
column28: Without light, elodea can't photosynthesize, but it keeps respiring, so it gives off CO₂ just like the snail. Tube 3 staying blue rules out the BTB changing on its own. Oxygen doesn't turn BTB yellow, and the tubes were sealed separately.
column29: What can a plant do in the dark, and what can't it do?

column9: In a fish tank full of plants, dissolved oxygen is highest in the late afternoon and lowest just before sunrise. What best explains this?
column14: The fish sleep at night and stop using oxygen
column15: Oxygen escapes from the water faster at night
column16: Plants carry out cellular respiration only in daylight
column17: All night the fish and the plants use oxygen for respiration, but the plants can't make oxygen without light
column28: During the day, photosynthesis adds oxygen faster than respiration uses it. At night photosynthesis stops, but both the fish and the plants keep respiring, so oxygen drops until sunrise. Fish and plants respire around the clock.
column29: Which process stops at night, and which keeps going?

column9: Which statements are true for BOTH a human and an oak tree? Select all that apply.
column14: They make their own glucose using sunlight
column15: They use oxygen in cellular respiration
column16: They give off carbon dioxide from cellular respiration
column17: Their cells contain mitochondria
column19: They break down glucose to make ATP
column28: Both humans and oak trees carry out aerobic cellular respiration in mitochondria: they use oxygen, break down glucose for ATP, and give off carbon dioxide. Only the tree has chloroplasts and makes glucose from sunlight. The common mistake is thinking a plant's photosynthesis replaces respiration.
column29: Sort each statement: respiration (everyone) or photosynthesis (plants only)?

column9: A respirometer is a sealed tube of sprouting peas with a chemical inside that absorbs all the carbon dioxide the peas give off. A colored drop of water in a thin side tube slowly moves toward the peas. What is the respirometer measuring?
column14: How much carbon dioxide the peas release into the air
column15: How much water the peas absorb
column16: How fast the peas use up oxygen in cellular respiration
column17: How fast the peas make oxygen by photosynthesis
column28: The chemical removes the CO₂ the peas make, so the only gas change left is oxygen being used up. As the gas volume shrinks, the drop is pulled toward the peas. The faster it moves, the faster the peas are respiring. It can't measure CO₂ release because that gas is absorbed.
column29: If CO₂ is removed, which gas change is left to move the drop?

column9: A scientist measures the carbon dioxide given off by mice: resting 1.0, walking 2.5, running 6.0 units per minute. Which other measurement would most likely ALSO increase from resting to running?
column14: Number of mitochondria in each muscle cell
column16: Oxygen used per minute
column17: Glucose stored in the mice's muscles
column28: More CO₂ means the cells are doing more cellular respiration, which also uses more oxygen. Stored glucose would go down as it's burned, and breaths would come faster (less time between them). The number of mitochondria doesn't change during one run; the mitochondria they already have just work faster.
column29: Carbon dioxide out and oxygen in are linked by the equation.

column9: A cell has plenty of oxygen but completely runs out of glucose and every other fuel. What happens to its ATP production by cellular respiration?
column14: It switches to making glucose from carbon dioxide
column15: It stops, because there is no fuel to break down, even with plenty of oxygen
column16: It keeps going, making ATP from oxygen alone
column17: It keeps making 36 ATP per minute no matter what
column28: Respiration needs BOTH reactants. Oxygen only helps release energy that is stored in fuel; it doesn't contain usable energy by itself. With no fuel, the reaction stops. Animal cells can't make glucose from carbon dioxide.
column29: Respiration has two reactants. What happens if one is missing?

column9: A student wants to test whether crickets give off more carbon dioxide when they are warmer. Which plan is the best test?
column14: Use a small jar at the cold temperature and a large jar at the warm temperature
column15: Put 5 crickets in a cold jar and 20 crickets in a warm jar
column16: Measure CO₂ in one warm jar only
column17: Put the same number of similar-size crickets in identical sealed jars at different temperatures and measure CO₂ after the same amount of time
column28: A fair test changes only one variable (temperature) and keeps everything else the same: number and size of crickets, jar size, and time. Changing the number of crickets or the jar size gives a second cause for any difference, and one jar alone has nothing to compare to.
column29: A fair test changes only one thing.

column9: Scientists let a mouse breathe air in which the O₂ gas was made with a special "tagged" kind of oxygen atom that they can trace. After cellular respiration, where in the mouse's body would most of the tagged oxygen show up?
column14: In glucose stored in its liver
column16: In the carbon dioxide it breathes out
column17: In water made by its cells
column28: The O₂ you breathe in is used at the end of the electron transport chain, where it picks up electrons and hydrogen and becomes water. Experiments like this one showed that the oxygen in exhaled CO₂ comes from glucose (and water), not from inhaled O₂. Choosing carbon dioxide is the classic mistake.
column29: Where exactly is O₂ used, and what does it form there?

column9: A mouse sealed alone in a glass jar runs out of oxygen, and so does a plant sealed alone in a dark jar. But a mouse and a plant sealed together in a jar in the light can both survive much longer. Which explanation uses both processes correctly?
column14: The mouse's respiration gives off CO₂ the plant uses for photosynthesis, and the plant's photosynthesis gives off O₂ the mouse uses for respiration
column15: The plant gives the mouse ATP through the air
column16: Both the mouse and the plant make oxygen
column17: The mouse gives the plant glucose to use
column28: Respiration and photosynthesis cycle the same gases. The mouse uses O₂ and releases CO₂; in the light the plant uses CO₂ and releases O₂. ATP and glucose don't move through the air between organisms, and only the plant makes oxygen.
column29: What does each organism give off that the other one needs?

column9: A drug blocks the electron transport chain in a person's cells. Which effects would you predict? Select all that apply.
column14: The cells start making glucose
column16: The cells stop needing ATP
column17: The cells use more oxygen
column28: The electron transport chain makes most of the ATP, is where O₂ is used, and is where water is formed. Block it and all three drop. Animal cells can't make glucose this way, and cells always need ATP, which is why such drugs are poisons.
column29: List the three things the electron transport chain does, then predict what happens to each.

column9: A cell completely breaks down 2 glucose molecules. Not counting ATP, how many product molecules (carbon dioxide plus water) does it make in all?
column28: One glucose makes 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O = 12 product molecules. Two glucose make 2 × 12 = 24. A common mistake is answering 12 by counting for only one glucose, or counting just one of the two products.
column29: Count CO₂ and H₂O for one glucose, then double it.

column9: A student claims, "The mass of a sealed jar of sprouting seeds will go down as the seeds respire, because matter gets used up." What is the best response?
column14: The jar's total mass stays the same, because the atoms are only rearranged into CO₂ and water that stay inside the sealed jar
column15: The mass will go down because oxygen is destroyed
column16: The mass will go up, because the seeds make new atoms
column17: The student is right; respiration turns matter into energy
column28: In a sealed jar nothing can enter or leave, so the total mass stays the same. The seeds lose mass as they burn stored food, but that mass becomes CO₂ and water vapor in the jar's air. Atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.
column29: Can atoms leave a sealed jar?

column9: Some people inherit a condition in which their mitochondria don't work well. Which parts of the body would most likely show symptoms first?
column14: Muscles and the brain, which use large amounts of ATP
column16: Fat tissue
column17: The outer layer of dead skin cells
column28: Mitochondria make most of a cell's ATP, so the organs that use the most energy (muscles, the heart, and the brain) are hit hardest. Hair, nails, and the outer layer of skin are made of dead cells, and fat cells use little energy.
column29: Which tissues have the biggest ATP demand?
